strengths: Excellent hardware-model co-design addressing the most critical bottlenecks of modern fine-grained and sparse MoE architectures (such as DeepSeek-V3 style models).

Comprehensive system-level optimizations spanning mathematical graph reformulations, low-level CUDA kernels (utilizing advanced features of Hopper and Blackwell like cp.async, TMA, and TMEM), and an efficient register-based top-K sorting kernel.

Very impressive performance gains: up to 1.86x training throughput speedup over ScatterMoE, and a reduction in activation memory by up to 45%. The end-to-end evaluation on 64 H100s shows highly competitive throughput, making it practically useful.

The proposed 'token rounding' routing algorithm is well-justified, elegantly solving the tile quantization/padding issue in sparse MoEs. It is backed by robust NLP downstream evaluations on 11 tasks across multiple models (0.5B to 1.8B params) trained on up to 100B tokens, proving it preserves model quality.
Extremely thorough profiling and analysis of memory bandwidth, TFLOPS, and kernel breakdown, showing a deep understanding of GPU architecture.
weaknesses: Highly specialized to NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell architectures (using TMEM, TMA, cluster-level synchronization, etc.), which limits immediate portability to other platforms like AMD GPUs or TPUs.

The downstream evaluation of the token rounding method, while extensive for a systems paper, is still conducted on relatively small models (up to 1.8B parameters) and token counts compared to today's frontier MoEs.
Some figures and tables (e.g., Figures 6, 13, 14) are extremely dense and contain small, packed text, which can make reading and digesting the exact details slightly challenging.

strengths: A highly timely and impactful contribution. MoE architectures (especially fine-grained ones like DeepSeek V3) have become the industry standard, and optimizing their systems efficiency is of paramount importance.

Excellent hardware-software co-design. The paper cleverly combines mathematical reformulations of the backward pass (eliminating the need to cache Y and dY) with low-level CUDA optimizations (gather/epilogue fusion, Ping-Pong scheduling) and algorithmic modifications (Token Rounding).

Outstanding performance improvements. Achieving up to 45% activation memory savings and up to 1.86x compute throughput improvement compared to highly optimized baselines like ScatterMoE and MoMoE is highly impressive.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation. The authors benchmark multiple model scales (1.4B to 120B) and validate downstream model quality across 11 tasks, proving that Token Rounding maintains high accuracy while saving significant padding overhead.

Clear, well-written, and technically deep. The paper does not shy away from low-level architectural details (TMA, cp.async, Hopper, and Blackwell GPU features) and provides a clear description of all techniques.
weaknesses: The evaluation of the Blackwell GPU optimizations (such as the 2-CTA cluster relay mechanism) is described conceptually but lacks concrete empirical performance figures on Blackwell hardware, with all major benchmarks performed on Hopper (H100).

The Token Rounding (TR) method introduces additional routing logic and sorting. While the overhead is shown to be low, the reliance on a fixed tile size (e.g., 128) might make the method less portable to non-NVIDIA accelerators or alternative kernels with different tile requirements.
Although a default choice (NR-f) is recommended, the multiple variants of token rounding subroutines (NR-f, SR-f, NR-s, Balance-f, etc.) add complexity and hyperparameter tuning choices for the user.

strengths: Strong motivation addressing critical hardware bottlenecks (IO cost, activation memory, and padding waste) in modern, state-of-the-art fine-grained and highly sparse MoE architectures (e.g., DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2).

Impressive hardware-software co-design approach that successfully combines low-level GPU kernel fusions (using CuTe-DSL) with algorithmic innovations like activation-efficient backward passes and Token Rounding (TR) routing.
State-of-the-art implementation details targeting both NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell architectures, including a novel relay-warp mechanism to bypass the 2-CTA cluster architectural limits on Blackwell.

Exceptional and rigorous empirical evaluation across multiple model scales (from 1.4B up to 120B parameters), demonstrating substantial training throughput improvements (up to 1.86x over ScatterMoE) and constant activation memory footprint.

Thorough validation of the proposed Token Rounding routing method through actual pre-training runs (up to 100B tokens) evaluated across 11 NLP downstream benchmarks, showing robust performance despite training-inference discrepancy.
weaknesses: There is an inherent discrepancy between training (which uses hardware-tile-aligned Token Rounding) and inference (which switches back to standard top-K routing because TR is not easily compatible with autoregressive generation). Although empirical results show minimal quality loss, a deeper theoretical analysis or investigation of potential edge cases (e.g., long-context retrieval, out-of-distribution settings) is largely missing.

The low-level performance optimizations (such as cp.async, TMA, TMEM, 2-CTA clusters, and Hopper-specific Ping-Pong scheduling) are deeply tied to NVIDIA's latest architectures. This limits the portability of these techniques to other accelerators (like AMD GPUs or Google TPUs) or older GPU generations.
In Section 1 (page 3, line 3), the GitHub link is left completely blank ('The GitHub link is .'), which appears to be a writing oversight.

The codebase relies on highly fused mega-kernels written in CuTe-DSL, which dramatically increases implementation complexity, making it difficult for the community to maintain, debug, or integrate into standard PyTorch/Megatron-LM frameworks.

strengths: Excellent hardware-software co-design: The paper elegantly addresses both the kernel-level memory/compute bottlenecks and the algorithmic aspect of MoE routing (via tile-aware Token Rounding) to perfectly align with modern GPU architecture requirements (like 128-sized tiles in grouped GEMMs).

Substantial memory optimization: Redesigning the computation graph to bypass caching of intermediate activations ($Y$ and $dY$) for router gradient computation successfully decouples activation memory footprint from expert granularity, matching the memory footprint of a dense model.

Comprehensive, state-of-the-art benchmarks: Performance is thoroughly validated across both NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and the newest Blackwell (B300) GPUs. The proposed method demonstrates significant throughput (TFLOPS) improvements and memory savings compared to highly optimized baselines like DeepGEMM, ScatterMoE, and MoMoE.

Strong empirical downstream validation: Unlike typical systems papers that evaluate only raw speed, this work validates the Token Rounding routing algorithm through actual model pre-training and downstream task evaluations (up to 1.8B parameters), showing no degradation in perplexity or downstream accuracy compared to standard top-$K$ choice routing.
weaknesses: Algorithmic scale of evaluation: While the downstream validation up to 1.8B parameters is highly appreciated, it remains to be seen if the Token Rounding approach scales without any quality degradation when training extremely large frontier MoEs (e.g., >100B parameters) on trillions of tokens.

Interplay with Expert Parallelism (EP): The paper focuses heavily on single-node or FSDP-2 settings. Mixture-of-Experts training at scale typically relies heavily on EP, which introduces communication overhead (e.g., `all-to-all`). More discussion or profiling on how SonicMoE behaves when combined with EP communication-computation overlapping would strengthen the work.

High engineering complexity and maintenance: Implementing custom low-level kernels in CuTe-DSL with specific scheduling (like Blackwell TMEM stage management and Hopper Ping-Pong warpgroups) makes the system highly specialized and potentially harder to maintain or port as future GPU architectures evolve.

strengths: The paper presents a very comprehensive hardware-software co-design approach for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, combining low-level GPU kernel optimizations (overlapping IO with MMA, kernel fusion) with high-level routing modifications (token rounding).

Impressive empirical results with significant speedups (e.g., 43% on forward and 83% on backward compared to DeepGEMM/ScatterMoE on Hopper, and clear gains on Blackwell) and up to a 45% reduction in peak activation memory.

The proposed 'token rounding' algorithm elegantly addresses the tile quantization issue (compute waste due to padding in Grouped GEMMs) for highly sparse MoEs, demonstrating both throughput improvements and downstream accuracy retention across multiple tasks.

Exceptional and thorough benchmarking across different GPU architectures (NVIDIA H100 and B300) and model scales ranging from 1.4B to 120B parameters, which lends high credibility to the systems-level claims.
Commitment to open-sourcing the implementation, which will be of significant value to the community working on large-scale MoE training.
weaknesses: The hardware optimizations are highly specific to modern NVIDIA architectures (Hopper and Blackwell) and rely heavily on specific features like TMA, TMEM, and cluster-level synchronization. This limits the portability of the proposed optimizations to other hardware accelerators (such as TPUs or AMD GPUs).

The token rounding routing requires computing token frequencies over a microbatch, which introduces a train-test mismatch since evaluation/inference typically uses standard top-K routing. While the paper demonstrates that switching back to standard top-K during evaluation works well as a drop-in replacement, more analysis on this mismatch's boundary cases would strengthen the paper.

The effectiveness and robustness of token rounding depend on the microbatch size and tile size ratio ($T_e/M_{tile} \ge 2$). In scenarios with small microbatches or extreme sparsity where this ratio drops to 1, a noticeable degradation in downstream quality is observed.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and timely problem: accelerating the training of fine-grained and sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) models, which have become the de facto standard for state-of-the-art LLMs (e.g., DeepSeek-V3).

Excellent hardware-software co-design approach that targets three different bottlenecks: activation memory scaling (via mathematical reformulation of the backward pass), IO overhead (via low-level GPU kernel fusion and overlapping), and tile quantization (via an algorithmic token-rounding routing strategy).

Exceptional engineering depth and novelty in low-level GPU programming. Leveraging Hopper's asynchronous features and Blackwell's new Tensor Memory (TMEM) architectures with customized warp/threadblock schedulers shows state-of-the-art systems engineering.

Very thorough and rigorous empirical evaluation. The paper benchmarks throughput (TFLOPS, tokens/day) and activation memory across multiple model scales (up to 120B and a 685B configuration) on both H100 and B300 (Blackwell) GPUs. It compares against a comprehensive set of baselines including ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron-LM, and DeepGEMM.

The proposed token-rounding algorithm is validated not just for speed, but also for downstream accuracy on 11 tasks and validation perplexity across multiple parameter scales, demonstrating no loss in model quality.
weaknesses: Sensitivity of Token Rounding to Microbatch Size: The token rounding (TR) algorithm is dependent on having a sufficient number of tokens per expert per microbatch ($\bar{T}_e$). The ablation studies in Table 7 and 8 show that when this ratio is low ($\bar{T}_e/M_{tile} = 1$), there is a noticeable degradation in perplexity and downstream task accuracy.

Strict Hardware Specificity: The low-level optimizations (such as TMEM staging on Blackwell and cp.async cluster-level synchronization) are highly tailored to NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell architectures. This makes the system optimizations difficult to port to other accelerators (e.g., AMD GPUs or TPUs).

Train-Test Mismatch: Since TR is designed for training and is not directly compatible with autoregressive generation, the model must switch back to vanilla token-choice routing during inference. Although evaluated to have a minor impact, this introduces a slight discrepancy between training and inference.

Dense Presentation: The paper is extremely dense and packs a massive amount of low-level GPU architecture and scheduling details into the main text, which may make it less accessible to a general machine learning audience.
